query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding tantalum (Ta) in appropriate amounts to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will promote the in-situ formation of a continuous CrTaO4-based oxide scale that protects the alloy from high-temperature oxygen attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in its standard composition which shows moderate oxidation resistance and tends to form non-protective or less continuous oxides when exposed at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by incorporating additional Ta (while maintaining sufficient Cr content) to enable CrTaO4 scale formation during high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Exposed isothermally at around 1100 °C for prolonged durations (up to 200 hours) in an oxygen-rich (or air) atmosphere aimed to simulate extreme operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing CrTaO4-based oxide layer on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The added Ta reacts with available Cr during oxidation to form CrTaO4, a thermodynamically stable oxide that acts as an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion. This barrier reduces further oxidation, decelerating the oxidation kinetics (observed as a shift from exponential to parabolic kinetics) compared to alloys that do not form a protective scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ta-enhanced RHEA is expected to exhibit a lower mass gain during high-temperature oxidation tests (indicating improved oxygen resistance) as well as a more uniform and dense protective oxide scale compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated RHEA, which under identical high-temperature conditions, forms less protective oxide scales (e.g., incomplete Cr or mixed oxides) resulting in higher oxidation rates (weight gain) and poorer long-term stability.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated for high-temperature conditions (~1100 °C) in oxidizing atmospheres; its effectiveness at lower temperatures or under different environmental conditions is uncertain and would require further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement is not precisely defined and may vary with the exact alloy composition and Ta content. It is uncertain if there is an optimal window for Ta addition beyond which other detrimental effects could arise.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA samples: one with the standard composition and the other with additional Ta added. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for 200 hours in an oxygen-rich atmosphere. Characterize the oxidation kinetics through mass gain measurements and examine the surface/oxide scale using microscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect the presence and morphology of CrTaO4.
measurements: Phase identification and morphology of the oxide scale via XRD and SEM
Parabolic oxidation rate constants derived from weight gain data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Ta-enhanced alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and fails to exhibit the formation of a dense, continuous CrTaO4-based oxide scale compared to the untreated alloy under the same experimental conditions.

cited_evidence.text:
An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
